title: Learning a Task-Adaptive Low-Dimensional Semantic Space for Improved Visual Classification
claim: Aligning visual features to a generic text-encoder space limits separability; constructing a task-adaptive space first yields discriminative, compact, semantically faithful targets.
layout: 2 side-by-side panels, left-to-right flows, shaded construction box in right panel
description: Two framed panels compare pipelines for text-guided visual classification. Panel (a), labeled 'Alignment to text encoder semantic space', shows a visual encoder (trapezoid with a flame icon, meaning trainable) feeding an Alignment box (also flame) that outputs into a scatter of mixed red, yellow and blue dots, which is the text-encoder semantic space. A text encoder (snowflake, frozen) sends its embedding straight to that same space. Panel (b), 'Alignment to Task-adaptive Semantic Space (TaSS)', has a frozen visual encoder and an Alignment box that outputs into a box with three tight, well-separated clusters of red, blue and yellow crosses. Below, a frozen text encoder feeds a scatter, then a peach 'TaSS construction' box lists three goals: inter-class separation, multi-prototype compactness and semantic fidelity preservation. An arrow carries the result up into TaSS. Blue arrows and dimension labels d_v and d_E run throughout.
caption: Overview of text-guided visual classification. (a) Alignment to the original text-encoder semantic space that is dimensionally mismatched with visual features is not optimized for discrimination, limiting class separability. (b) Our method aligns frozen visual features to \paperabb{} constructed from the text-encoder space, with controllable dimensionality, enhanced inter-class separation, multi-prototype compactness, and semantic preservation.
abstract: Semantic visual classification commonly aligns visual embeddings with semantic spaces induced by pretrained text encoders. However, such spaces are typically high-dimensional, weakly aligned with visual feature geometry, and insufficiently discriminative for downstream classification tasks. We propose TaSS, a framework for learning a task-adaptive low-dimensional semantic space that preserves semantic structure while explicitly optimizing class separability. TaSS is constructed through a parameterized geometry transformation of pretrained text embeddings that enlarges inter-class margins via distance reshaping and improves intra-class compactness through prototype-preserving semantic constraints. The resulting semantic space maintains meaningful semantic relationships while producing a discriminative geometry tailored for classification. Frozen visual encoder features are subsequently aligned to TaSS using a lightweight MLP, enabling improved discriminative learning without fine-tuning pretrained backbones. We further provide theoretical analysis showing that TaSS preserves semantic consistency while enforcing enhanced inter-class separation and controlled intra-class variance. Extensive experiments on skeleton-based human action recognition, video classification, and image classification benchmarks demonstrate consistent improvements over existing semantic alignment approaches, with gains exceeding 3 percentage points on average and up to 8.5 points on challenging datasets.
